newsitem.title: JAPAN: Volume rise brings hope to Tokyo forex market.
newsitem.headline: Volume rise brings hope to Tokyo forex market.

text.p: It may be too early to break out the champagne, but with this year's trading volume in the Tokyo currency market likely to hit a six-year high, dealers are hopeful the market's long decline may have come to a halt.
"I believe we've actually seen the turn," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"There were times when they were saying the Tokyo market was fading as a centre, but the big investment base is still here, as are the customers."
But others felt the cost of operating in Japan and the country's feeble economic recovery meant a turnaround had not happened.
"I have a sense that volume is up, but no strong feeling that the market is actually recovering," said Hideki Naito, managing analyst at MMS International.
Citing onerous regulations, high business costs, and lagging Japanese economic recovery, he added: "I don't really know how appealing this market is yet."

According to data compiled by the Foreign Exchange and Money Brokers Association, the volume of dollar-for-yen spot and swap transactions through brokers to the end of October was around $4.84 trillion, compared with $4.31 trillion the same time last year.

And with trading volume at a fairly brisk level through much of November, including this year's daily turnover high of $41.6 billion on November 7, a rise above 1995's total $5.1 trillion seems virtually assured.

The volume last year was the highest since the market's all-time peak of $5.96 billion in 1990, but most dealers felt 1995's gain was only temporary, the result of a volatile trading year during which the dollar fell as low as 79.75 yen.
This year, the dollar rose slowly from around 104 yen in January to a high of 114.92 yen on October 29, with frequent consolidation and small corrections but none of 1995's turmoil.

In combination with record low Japanese interest rates, this stability helped lure Japanese operators into heavy investments in high-yielding foreign securities, which meant selling yen for dollars and other foreign currencies, and kept the volume at a good level throughout the year.

Particularly notable was active investment in Australian dollars, which hit a four-year high against the yen in November due to the steady issue of dual currency samurai bonds. Sterling and the mark also made phenomenal gains.

The thirst for overseas investment appears likely to continue, dealers said. Many of Japan's major life insurers announced on Wednesday that they plan to beef up their overseas investments in the second half of this fiscal year.

"In the past, there's been concern that Tokyo was a dollar/yen-only local market. But now interest is expanding to a lot of other currencies, and this has been positive for the market as a whole," said Masayoshi Aoki, a director at the Tokyo Forex Co Ltd, one of Japan's largest currency brokers.
He added that behind the increased foreign investment appeared to lie a shift in Japanese investor psychology showing they are now much more aggressive about taking risks.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Landon said he suspects the recent shrinkage of Japan's current account surplus may slow or even stop next year. "There will be a lot more capital to recycle and invest overseas, and if the U.S. doesn't change its policy to work for a sharply lower dollar, (investment) is likely to continue, even if the dollar weakens a bit."

Regulations remain a problem for Tokyo, and while most dealers agreed the government's recent "Big Bang" financial deregulation proposals were likely to inject life into the market, they were still wary.
"The idea is very good, but stretching it out to 2001 is just too long," Naito at MMS said.
